title: Java String Pool and String Interning
summary: Java caches all string literals in a special heap area called the String Pool. This is why two string literals with the same value share the same memory address, but two 'new String()' objects do not — a classic and frequently tested interview topic.
detailedHtml:
The String Pool (also called the String Constant Pool) is a special storage area inside the Java heap where the JVM caches string literals to avoid creating duplicate objects.

How it works

  • When you write String a = "hello", the JVM first checks the pool. If "hello" already exists, it returns the same reference. If not, it creates a new entry in the pool.
  • When you write String b = new String("hello"), you force a new object to be created on the heap, bypassing the pool entirely.

The Critical Interview Gotcha

This is why == compares references (memory addresses) while .equals() compares content:

String a = "hello";
String b = "hello";
String c = new String("hello");

System.out.println(a == b);        // true  — same pool reference
System.out.println(a == c);        // false — c is a new heap object
System.out.println(a.equals(c));   // true  — same content

// Force c into the pool:
String d = c.intern();
System.out.println(a == d);        // true — d now points to the pool entry

Production Rule

Always use .equals() to compare String values. Never use ==. The == check for Strings is only valid if you deliberately want to check if two variables point to the exact same object in memory.

title: Comparable vs Comparator — When to Use Which
summary: Java gives you two ways to sort objects: Comparable (the object defines its own natural order) and Comparator (an external strategy object defines the order). Knowing which to use — and when — is a common Java interview question.
detailedHtml:
Both interfaces define how objects should be ordered, but they serve different design purposes.

Comparable — Natural Ordering

Implement Comparable<T> inside the class itself when there is one obvious, natural way to sort that class (e.g., sort employees by ID, sort products by price).

public class Employee implements Comparable<Employee> {
    private int id;
    private String name;

    @Override
    public int compareTo(Employee other) {
        return Integer.compare(this.id, other.id); // Natural order: by ID
    }
}

// Usage:
List<Employee> employees = new ArrayList<>();
Collections.sort(employees); // Uses Comparable automatically

Comparator — Flexible External Ordering

Use Comparator<T> when you need multiple different sorting strategies, or when you cannot modify the class itself.

// Sort by name, then by ID as a tiebreaker
Comparator<Employee> byNameThenId = Comparator
        .comparing(Employee::getName)
        .thenComparingInt(Employee::getId);

employees.sort(byNameThenId);

The Rule of Thumb

  • Comparable = The class knows its own natural order. Built-in, one way only.
  • Comparator = An external rule book you hand to the sort. Flexible and reusable.

title: Java Exception Hierarchy: Checked vs Unchecked
summary: Not all Java exceptions are equal. The distinction between Checked and Unchecked exceptions defines whether the compiler forces you to handle them. This is one of the most fundamental Java concepts tested in interviews at every level.
detailedHtml:
Java's exception system is a class hierarchy rooted at Throwable:

Throwable
+-- Error              (JVM-level: OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError)
+-- Exception
    +-- RuntimeException  (Unchecked: NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException)
    +-- IOException        (Checked: FileNotFoundException, SQLException)

Checked Exceptions

The compiler forces you to handle these. They represent recoverable external failures — file not found, network timeout.

// You MUST handle this — the compiler will not compile otherwise
public void readFile(String path) throws IOException {
    Files.readAllLines(Paths.get(path));
}

Unchecked Exceptions (RuntimeException)

The compiler does not force you to handle these. They represent programming bugs — null pointer, bad arguments. Fix the bug; don't catch it.

// Will crash at runtime if name is null
public void greet(String name) {
    System.out.println(name.toUpperCase()); // NullPointerException
}

Golden Rule

Never catch Exception broadly. Always catch the most specific exception type. Use try-with-resources for anything implementing AutoCloseable.

title: HashMap Internals: How get() and put() Actually Work
summary: HashMap is the most-used data structure in Java, and also the most mis-understood. Understanding how it uses hashCode(), equals(), and bucket chaining is essential for every Java developer interview.
detailedHtml:
A HashMap internally uses an array of buckets (linked lists or trees). Every key-value pair is stored in a specific bucket determined by the key's hash code.

Step-by-step: put(key, value)

  1. Call key.hashCode() to get an integer hash.
  2. Apply a bitwise operation to spread the hash across the bucket array index.
  3. Go to that bucket. If it is empty, store the entry there.
  4. If the bucket has entries (a collision), iterate and compare using key.equals() to find if the key already exists. If yes, update. If no, append.
// The CONTRACT you MUST follow: if a.equals(b) is true, then
// a.hashCode() MUST equal b.hashCode(). Breaking this breaks HashMap!
public class Point {
    int x, y;

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        Point p = (Point) o;
        return this.x == p.x && this.y == p.y;
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(x, y); // Always override both!
    }
}

Interview Gotcha

If you override equals() but NOT hashCode(), two logically equal objects will go into different buckets and HashMap will behave incorrectly — failing to find keys it should find. Always override both together.

title: Java Generics: Type Erasure Explained
summary: Java Generics are a compile-time feature. At runtime, all generic type information is erased by the compiler — a process called Type Erasure. This is why you cannot create generic arrays or use instanceof with a generic type.
detailedHtml:
When the Java compiler processes generics, it replaces all type parameters with their bounds (or Object if unbounded) and inserts casts where necessary. This is called Type Erasure.

Before and after compilation

// What YOU write:
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Alice");
String name = names.get(0);

// What the COMPILER produces (after type erasure):
List names = new ArrayList();
names.add("Alice");
String name = (String) names.get(0); // Cast inserted automatically

Consequences of Type Erasure

  • You cannot do new T() or new T[] — the JVM does not know what T is at runtime.
  • You cannot do obj instanceof List<String> — only obj instanceof List is valid.
  • List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class at runtime: java.util.ArrayList.

Why did Java do this?

Type Erasure was chosen for backward compatibility. When generics were added in Java 5, pre-existing bytecode (compiled without generics) had to continue working without modification on the same JVM.
